newsitem.title: USA: Republicans accuse Clinton aides of falsehoods.
newsitem.headline: Republicans accuse Clinton aides of falsehoods.

text.p: A Republican-controlled House of Representatives subcommittee accused Clinton administration officials on Thursday of making possibly criminal false statements about U.S. policy on Iran's arming of Bosnians in 1994.

One Republican subcommittee member accused aides to President Bill Clinton of lying to allies, Congress and the U.S. public. But congressional Democrats called the subcommittee's allegation outrageous and unsupported.

An unclassified summary of the subcommittee's "Top Secret" report said "several administration officials gave false testimony to Congress on the development and implementation of the Iranian green light policy. ... The subcommittee is referring this matter to the Department of Justice for further criminal investigation."

Administration officials testified at congressional hearings that they decided in 1994 neither to approve nor oppose Croatia's plan to aid Iran's shipments of weapons to Moslem-led Bosnian government forces because they feared Bosnia would collapse without the arms.

Republicans said the decision was deceptive because the administration publicly opposed arms for Bosnia at the time and that it allowed Iran to gain influence in Bosnia. The summary was released by the Select Subcommittee on the U.S. Role in Iranian Arms Transfers to Croatia and Bosnia, a House International Relations Committee panel.

Democrats on the full committee issued a statement saying the finding was outrageous because U.S. officials disagreed only on "inconsequential details." They said they reviewed the classified evidence and found no false statements, no other wrongdoing and no harm to U.S. interests.

But Representative Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican and a member of the subcommittee, said: "The administration lied to our allies ... They lied to the Congress of the United States and they lied to the American people."

The subcommittee's chairman, Representative Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican, said more cautiously that the subcommittee was not accusing anyone of criminality and was only asking for a criminal investigation of discrepancies in testimony.
Hyde said he could not elaborate on the secret report but the discrepancies were between other administration officials and U.S. Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith on their instructions to him.

Officials suggested in public testimony that Galbraith and then U.S. Bosnia negotiator Charles Redman went beyond their orders to tell Croatian officials they "had no instructions" on the Iran arms by elaborating on what the words meant.

The summary also said, "There is evidence that Ambassador Galbraith played a significant supervisory role with respect to at least one Iranian weapons transshipment through Croatia ... To the extent he actively participated in the formation and execution of the Iranian arms pipeline, there is a high probability that he ... engaged in an unlawful covert action."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. policy succeeded in ending the war in Bosnia and the administration's decision on Iran arms was fully reported to Congress in 1995.
Noting that the congressional report was being released a month before the U.S. presidential election, Burns said, "I don't believe that's a coincidence."
